name: Tomas Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I am with the independent Work Futures Panel; we have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. What does an ordinary day on the lines look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go out from the North Ford depot with a basket truck, tools and a weather report that is often wrong. We replace worn fittings on the hill road and find faults when a farm loses power. I like leaving a lamp on in a house that was dark at breakfast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The ladders trouble my knees more than they used to. I have a vocational certificate and learned the trade beside older hands; now I spend too much time filling in forms for people who have never held a pole steady. Marta, my wife, can tell from my boots whether it has been a repair day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I would say the crews still have to climb the poles, and I would leave the computer promises to the office. A hillside power line has never fixed itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a paid house and more than half a year of household expenses set by. My wife Marta and I still watch the heating bill, but a quiet few years would let me finish the job on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the same repair rota and keep the monthly transfer from my pay into our savings account. When the first year of this supposed plateau passes, I would still be inspecting the crossarms myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved is the word. My knees complain on cold ladders, but I can see a path through to retirement without learning a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first thing you would change in your weekly spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would change nothing straightaway. Marta and I already choose a cheaper holiday if the house needs work, and we can still pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI app your daughter showed you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave it on the phone. I can read a pole number and tell the dispatcher where the broken line is without asking an app.

say: I would **keep** the repair rota and expect physical linework to continue.
I would call the small office savings useful, but I would not expect a new **repair method**.
think: Our **paid house** and savings give Marta and me room to finish work without rushing.
I still mind the **heating bill** and my knees, even if AI itself does very little.
do: Keep the **repair rota** and inspect crossarms on the hillside line by hand.
Transfer a fixed sum from each **monthly wage** into our savings account as before.
feel: **Relieved**, with an ordinary worry about my knees and the household heating bill.
S0.quote: A hillside power line has never fixed itself.
fieldNote: He grounds his confidence in a **paid house** and a practical understanding of line repairs.
His concern about ageing knees remains, though the **plateau** gives him time to finish work as planned.

steps.text: Keep the hillside repair rota and inspect crossarms by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger crew that a computer can book vans, but it cannot find a cracked insulator in sleet. I would also tell the office to show us a safe method before changing dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planners could be fewer, and management might then squeeze the field crews for faster calls. My own climbing hours might stay, yet the overtime that lifts my pay could thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the dispatcher for the next winter rota and compare the overtime with our household budget. If it falls, Marta and I would postpone replacing the kitchen cupboards rather than borrow for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, leaning anxious when I think about overtime. We have savings, but I dislike having the price of my work decided by a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your pay is exposed first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The storm overtime. I would still have base pay if I keep my post, but losing those shifts would delay the kitchen work. Storm overtime made our larger household repairs comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new dispatch software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the screen only if the company makes it part of the job. I would ask a colleague to show me the buttons, not sign up for an AI course.

say: A computer may **book vans**, but I would insist the depot proves any new dispatch method is safe.
I would tell the crew that **storm repairs** still need trained hands at the pole.
think: The office may cut planners and then press crews to handle **more calls** per shift.
My **overtime** could shrink even while my base job and the household savings stay intact.
do: Ask the **dispatcher** for the winter rota and compare likely overtime with our budget.
Postpone the **kitchen cupboards** if overtime falls, without taking on a loan.
feel: **Anxious** about losing overtime and having a screen set the pace of field work.
S1.quote: Storm overtime made our larger household repairs comfortable.
fieldNote: His public safety argument also protects his **overtime** and control of work pace.
He has a sizeable cushion, but speaks of a possible **income cut** in concrete household terms.

steps.text: Postpone replacement kitchen cupboards if storm overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the company cannot replace a climbing crew with a talking box in 2028. I would want a proper trial before any robot went near a live wire in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning office could change almost at once, and my pole work might follow three years later. I could be sixty three when those robots come, close to leaving anyway, but I cannot assume my employer will keep every crew until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check our retirement figures with Marta this month, including what happens if overtime ends. If my field hours are cut once thinking AI arrives, I would apply for another line crew nearby before spending the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have a way out, but the short gap between an office cut and the robots is enough to make sleep lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would make you look for another crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If two monthly rosters in a row show no overtime and fewer field calls, I would start asking at the other utilities. One lean month could just be weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots if the job remained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would work while the hours and my knees allow it. Checking whether we can afford to retire from linework is preparation, not a decision to leave the crew.

say: A **2028 thinking system** cannot climb poles, and I would demand a proper field trial before 2031 robots.
I would tell the crew that safety cannot rest on an **office demonstration**.
think: Planning jobs could go first, and my **field hours** might shrink before capable robots arrive.
Our **savings** buy time, yet the short transition could still disrupt my last working years.
do: Check **retirement figures** with Marta this month against an end to overtime.
Apply to **nearby line crews** after two reduced monthly rosters, if my field hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** because I could lose hours before I am ready to stop work.
S2.quote: Checking whether we can afford to retire from linework is preparation, not a decision to leave the crew.
fieldNote: He distinguishes planning for a gap from an actual **early retirement** decision.
His threshold is two weak rosters, and plenty of **nearby crews** give him an alternative.

steps.text: Apply to nearby line crews after two reduced monthly rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the company time to test equipment with real lineworkers present. A robot in 2034 would still need to prove it can handle bent poles and bad weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034 I would be past the age at which I hope to finish. The thinking system in 2031 might change my call sheets, but climbing is most of my day and I expect to keep earning until then if my health holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the job and ask my supervisor each autumn for the following year field staffing plan. I would also increase our monthly savings transfer from wages by what we currently spend on the second car, once Marta agrees we can sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my own pay. I still dislike the thought of the apprentices having fewer years to learn their trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you sell the second car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After Marta and I have checked that one car covers her errands and my shifts. If it does not, I will leave the transfer as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell an apprentice to learn faults from people and keep a record of repairs. I cannot promise an apprentice a power-line field job in 2034.

say: I would ask for **field trials** with working crews before any 2034 robot touched a line.
I would tell apprentices to learn **fault finding** from people while those people are still here.
think: I expect to earn through **2031** because climbing is most of my work and my health may hold.
The **2034 robots** could arrive after I have already left regular line work.
do: Keep the **lineworker job** while health and field shifts hold.
Increase the **monthly savings** transfer from wages if selling our second car works for Marta.
feel: **Calm** about my pay, with concern for apprentices facing a shorter field career.
S3.quote: I cannot promise an apprentice a power-line field job in 2034.
fieldNote: He expects the robot date to fall beyond his own **working horizon**.
His extra saving depends on a practical **one-car test** with Marta, rather than an assumed sale.

steps.text: Keep taking field shifts while health and staffing hold
Increase monthly savings from wages if Marta agrees to sell the second car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years is long enough to finish an apprenticeship and pass on the craft properly. I would still ask who signs off a robot work on a live line in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I should have retired before the thinking AI arrives in 2036 if things go as planned. The paid house and our savings make that a choice, though Marta and I must still keep the place sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the present crew for the next year and show the new apprentice how to test a dead line before touching it. I would keep the retirement date we have pencilled in, subject to my health and the household figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for myself. The slow timetable lets me close my tool box in the usual way, though the trade will look different for someone younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will you leave earlier because of the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I plan to leave on the date Marta and I already discussed, if our accounts permit it. The AI date does not bring my exit forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the apprentice to remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the apprentice to check the isolation points personally. A neat printout cannot tell you a switch was labelled wrong in the rain.

say: A **ten-year lead** lets apprentices learn real line work before thinking AI and later robots arrive.
I would ask who is responsible for **signing off** repairs done by a 2039 robot.
think: I expect to have **retired** on our existing plan before the thinking AI date.
The **paid house** makes that plausible, although Marta and I still need to check the household figures.
do: Keep the **present crew** and show the apprentice how to test an isolated line.
Follow the **existing retirement plan** if health and household accounts permit it.
feel: **Calm** for myself, with a little grief for how the trade may change.
S4.quote: A neat printout cannot tell you a switch was labelled wrong in the rain.
fieldNote: His own exit is tied to the **existing plan**, so no early-retirement action is implied.
He spends the long lead time on **apprentice safety** rather than trying unfamiliar AI tools.

steps.text: Keep field shifts and teach the apprentice isolation checks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the office could change my rosters before a climbing robot is even ready. A written field staffing plan and clear repair trials with our crew would help me decide whether to stay or ask another utility for work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is liable if an automated plan sends a crew to a line that is still live. My savings protect the house; they do not protect an apprentice from a bad instruction.

headlineQuote: My savings protect the house; they do not protect an apprentice from a bad instruction.
portrait: **Tomas**, 58, is a mid-level lineworker with a vocational certificate, apprenticeship training and long experience on hill-road repairs.
He has a **paid house**, more than six months of savings, higher pay for the trade and nearby alternative line crews.
He avoids **AI tools** and trusts hands-on inspection, while accepting that reduced overtime could still change household choices.
The **2028 case** worries him most because planning changes could cut rosters years before robots can repair lines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** puts his field hours and overtime at risk before capable robots appear.
whatWouldHelp: A written **field staffing plan** and crew-led repair trials would let him judge whether to stay.
